title: Ethics: Theories of Right and Wrong

questions.question: Which level of ethics asks what moral claims mean and whether moral truths are objective?
questions.rationale: Metaethics studies the meaning and status of moral talk; normative ethics builds theories of right action, and applied ethics handles cases.

questions.question: Bentham's hedonic calculus measures pleasures by:
options: Intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent
questions.rationale: Bentham's felicific calculus ranks pleasures on seven dimensions, with each person counting for one and nobody for more than one.

questions.question: Mill distinguished higher from lower pleasures, illustrating with the line:
options: Pleasure is the absence of pain
Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied
questions.rationale: Mill ranked mental pleasures above bodily ones in quality, answering the objection that utilitarianism is a doctrine fit only for swine.

questions.question: The difference between act and rule utilitarianism is that:
options: Act utilitarianism rejects pleasure as the standard
Rule utilitarianism assesses rules by the consequences of their general adoption
Act utilitarianism only applies to governments
questions.rationale: Act utilitarians rate each act by its own consequences; rule utilitarians rate the rules whose general adoption has the best consequences.

questions.question: For Kant, the imperative 'Keep promises — always' differs from 'If you want to be trusted, keep promises' because the former is:
questions.rationale: Hypothetical imperatives bind conditionally on desires (if you want X); the categorical imperative commands unconditionally on universalizable maxims.

questions.question: Which principle is one of Rawls' two principles of justice as fairness?
options: The greatest good of the greatest number
The difference principle — inequalities allowed only if they benefit the worst off
questions.rationale: Chosen from an original position behind a veil of ignorance (A Theory of Justice, 1971): equal basic liberties, and inequalities only when they advantage the least well off.

questions.question: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean places courage between:
questions.rationale: Each virtue is a mean relative to us between deficiency and excess: courage sits between cowardice and rashness, generosity between stinginess and wastefulness.

questions.question: Phronesis, the master virtue in Aristotle's ethics, is:
options: Practical wisdom — the skill of finding the right act in context
questions.rationale: Because no rule anticipates every case, phronesis is the virtue that locates the mean and the right action in the circumstances.

questions.question: Carol Gilligan's care ethics, in In a Different Voice (1982), emphasises:
options: Relationships and responsiveness over abstract rule-following
questions.rationale: Gilligan argued that morality grows out of caring relationships and responsiveness to particular others, challenging purely rule- and principle-centred accounts.

questions.question: In the trolley case, what is the standard deontological verdict on diverting the trolley to kill one instead of five?
options: Pull the switch; the arithmetic is decisive
Do not pull; diverting the trolley uses the one person as a means to save the rest
Pull, if the one is old
questions.rationale: The utilitarian pulls (five over one); the Kantian objects that turning the trolley treats the one as a mere means — the case separates the theories.
